Game: This is a drawing, not a game: when the line through P turns, the new dot S always stays on the same circle.
How to play: Drag P, Q, A or B, or focus a dot and use the arrow keys. Choose circles or chord to change which dots you drag; tick the boxes for names and angle hints, and press Place diameter chord to see the longest line.
Adjust
Look for the math

Three circles and one line through P: as the line turns, the point where two extra lines cross never leaves the third circle. This is the second page in a family of applets about the same 1975 olympiad problem; its siblings use a tangent or a radical axis, while this one uses equal angles in isosceles triangles.

The points the picture builds

Two circles meet at P and Q. A chord through P ends at A on the first circle and B on the second. Their centres are E and F. The circumcircle C(O) goes through E, F and Q; it meets the first circle again at L and the second again at M. Lines AL and BM cross at S. "Adjust circles" rebuilds a circle when you drag its end; "Adjust chord" slides the end around the circle that is already drawn. Either way the other end is moved so A, P and B stay on one line.

What never changes

The page claims that S lies on C(O), that L, S, M and Q are concyclic, that QP cuts the angle LQM in half, and that S is the centre of the circle through A, B and Q. The last one explains the rest: if S is that centre, then SA = SB = SQ, and the circle ABQ has its centre on C(O). The equalities come from inscribed angles: for example angle ABS = angle PBM = angle PQM and angle BAS = angle PAL = angle PQL. The logic test checked all of them over thousands of configurations and found them true to about 1e-6 of the board size.

The diameter chord

For convenience the page moves A so that AQ is a diameter of the first circle. Then QS is a diameter of C(O) and BQ is a diameter of the second circle. Halves of those diameters give isosceles triangles EOQ and ASQ, so AS = QS; likewise BS = QS. Write the chord direction as a turn t away from the perpendicular to PQ. The length is AB = 2 |EF| cos(t), largest when t = 0 — exactly the diameter chord. A small trap: the original olympiad asks for the largest product AP×PB, and for unequal circles that product peaks at a slightly different chord. The page only says "longest segment" here, and that part is true.

What the checks found

A second transcription of the applet's own circle and intersection routines was compared with the port over a grid of starting points, circle centres and directions plus random cases; every constructed point agreed to 1e-8. The applet calls the diagram "Finished" when |2·QE − QA| < 0.01; the port keeps that exact test. One harmless quirk is worth knowing: with P and Q vertically aligned, sliding A along the line through P perpendicular to PQ keeps the angle APQ a right angle, so the diagram stays Finished even though A moves.

Press Place diameter chord, tick Show names, then drag A up a little: watch the green circle through A, B and Q shrink while its centre S stays on the dashed circle.
